items.summary: Kukui (candlenut) is the official state tree of Hawaii — a silver-leafed, fast-growing tree found in gulches and valleys throughout the islands. The oily nut is an important condiment in Hawaiian cuisine (inamona) — roasted and mixed with salt to season poke and traditional dishes. Every part of the tree has traditional uses.
items.safety_notes: Raw kukui nuts are TOXIC — they contain a powerful purgative oil and should never be eaten raw. The nut must be roasted (charred) before consumption in small quantities. Roasted kukui is a condiment, not a snack — consume only small amounts (1–4 nuts per serving). Excessive quantities cause severe gastrointestinal distress even after roasting.
items.source: University of Hawaii CTAHR; traditional Hawaiian use

sections.heading: Identification
sections.body: A large, fast-growing tree (30–60 ft) most easily identified by its distinctive silvery-grey foliage — the leaves have a pale, almost metallic appearance due to fine hairs. Leaves are maple-shaped, 3–5 lobed. Fruit is a round, green, fleshy drupe 1.5–2 inches across, containing 1–2 hard-shelled round nuts inside a very hard brown shell. Trees often seen in gulches, roadsides, and mesic forest.
tips: The silvery, pale grey-green foliage is visible from a distance and makes kukui easy to spot from a car.
Look for fallen green husks and cracked brown nuts on the ground beneath the tree.

sections.heading: Where & When
sections.body: Common in gulches and stream valleys throughout West Hawaii at lower to mid elevations. Concentrated along the deep gulches of North and South Kona. Widely planted as an ornamental. Nuts fall year-round but are most abundant in fall and winter. The silvery canopy is visible in most valleys on the western slope of Mauna Loa.
tips: The gulches of Keei, Napoopoo, and Kealakekua have abundant wild kukui.
Collect nuts from the ground — the outer fleshy husk should be rotted away to expose the brown shell.

sections.heading: Processing (Inamona)
sections.body: Crack the extremely hard shell with a hammer or nutcracker to extract the oily white kernel. Traditional inamona preparation: (1) Roast kernels in a dry pan over medium heat, stirring constantly, until dark brown to charred on the outside — 10–15 minutes. (2) Cool completely. (3) Chop finely or pound in a mortar with Hawaiian sea salt to a coarse paste. (4) Taste — it should be rich, bitter-umami, and savory. Use as a condiment for poke, poi, raw fish, and vegetables in very small amounts (¼–½ teaspoon per serving).
tips: Cracking kukui shells requires significant force — a bench vise or a heavy hammer on a concrete surface.
The charring is essential — it neutralizes the purgative compounds while developing umami flavor.
Inamona freezes well — make a batch and freeze in a small jar.

sections.heading: Preservation
sections.body: Raw kernels: shell and store raw kernels in the freezer for up to 1 year — they are extremely oily and go rancid quickly at room temperature. Inamona (roasted and salted): store in the freezer in a sealed jar for up to 6 months; refrigerator up to 4 weeks. Do not water bath or pressure can inamona — it is a high-fat product unsuitable for canning. The shell and outer husk have no edible preservation uses but historically were used as candles (hence 'candlenut').
tips: Always store any kukui product cold — the high oil content causes rancidity at room temperature within days.
Label kukui products clearly — the raw nut and the roasted nut look similar but have very different safety profiles.

items.name: Noni (Morinda citrifolia)
items.summary: Noni is a Polynesian canoe plant with a long history of medicinal and food use in Hawaii. The lumpy, pale yellow-white fruit has a famously pungent odor when ripe — often described as overripe cheese or a gym locker — but it has been used as a food of last resort and as a source of juice and medicine for centuries. Noni juice is now a commercial health product.
items.safety_notes: Noni is generally safe for healthy adults in moderate amounts. High doses of noni juice may interact with blood thinners (warfarin) and some medications. People with kidney disease should avoid it — noni is high in potassium. The strong odor is off-putting but not a safety indicator. Pregnant women should consult a physician before consuming noni.
items.source: University of Hawaii CTAHR; traditional Hawaiian use

sections.heading: Identification
sections.body: A small evergreen tree or shrub (10–20 ft) with very large, shiny, dark green, prominently veined oval leaves. Flowers are small and white, emerging from a oval bumpy fruit structure (the syncarps). Fruit is distinctive: oval, 2–4 inches, covered in irregular polygonal segments (like a lumpy pineapple), pale green turning yellowish-white when ripe. When fully ripe the fruit becomes translucent and soft with a strong, distinctive fermented cheese odor.
tips: The large, glossy, quilted leaves and the uniquely textured pale fruit make noni unmistakable.
The smell of a ripe noni is quite strong — experienced foragers can smell a tree in fruit from downwind.

sections.heading: Where & When
sections.body: Common throughout coastal West Hawaii below 1,500 feet elevation — in lava fields, coastal scrub, roadsides, parks, and disturbed areas. Often seen growing in pure lava with minimal soil. Fruits continuously year-round. One of the few fruit trees that tolerates the harsh dry coastal conditions of the Kona and Kohala lowlands.
tips: Noni thrives in the lava fields where little else grows — it's common along the Queen K Highway corridor.
Ripe fruit falls from the tree and can be collected from the ground.

sections.heading: Harvest & Edible Parts
sections.body: Harvest when the fruit is translucent and pale, just beginning to soften — or collect fallen fruit. The smell intensifies dramatically as it ripens. The flesh and juice are edible; seeds are large and not typically consumed. Many people prefer to blend ripe noni with other juices (pineapple, lilikoi) to make the flavor more palatable.
tips: If you are new to noni, start with a small amount mixed into juice — the flavor is an acquired taste.
The smell is strongest in the skin; some prefer to squeeze the juice through a cloth to separate it.

sections.heading: Preservation
sections.body: Traditional Hawaiian preservation of noni: (1) Fermented noni juice — place ripe fruit in a covered glass jar, the juice seeps out naturally over 4–8 weeks; strain and bottle; traditional medicinal use. (2) Dried noni slices — slice and dehydrate at 135°F 12–18 hours; the odor diminishes significantly when dried; store in airtight container. (3) Noni juice frozen in ice cube trays — blend ripe fruit with a little water, strain, freeze; add cubes to smoothies. (4) Noni-infused vinegar — place in apple cider vinegar for 4–6 weeks, strain, use as a health tonic.
tips: Fermented noni juice is the traditional method — the fermentation process mellows the flavor somewhat.
Freeze fresh noni juice immediately if you want to preserve the fresh taste rather than fermented.
